news_drafts.headline: Cambridgeshire children's services forecast to overspend by £12.657m in 2026/27, up from £11.451m
news_drafts.lead:
Cambridgeshire's Children, Education and Families directorate is forecast to overspend its 2026/27 budget by £12.657m, or 7.2%, outside the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools. The October finance monitoring report sets that against a net budget of £175.808m and a previous forecast variance of £11.451m. Spending to October was £92.247m.

The report says an overspend against the budget for the year "would need to be financed through general reserves, which have a minimum level for ongoing financial sustainability."

On the DSG, the same report shows a forecast variance for 2026/27 of £75.170m, up from £73.938m in the previous forecast. The DSG line carries a net budget of nil, and spending to October was £46.784m. The extract of the paper provided does not explain the DSG position.

The committee also has a report on education construction contracts. It says the Isleham Primary School project will be funded from Schools Condition Grant, S106 developer contributions, Early Years Capital Grant and High Needs Provision Capital Allocation. The work covers boiler, window and playground surfacing replacement, early years expansion, refurbishing the old swimming pool block and extra provision for special educational needs and disabilities. Target start on site is July 2027, with completion targeted for September 2027.

news_drafts.headline: Cambridgeshire's schools deficit reached £96.3m at March 2026; £63.3m more forecast for 2026-27
news_drafts.lead:
Cambridgeshire County Council's cumulative deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, rose from £62.851m to £96.3m over 2025-26, after an in-year deficit of £33.406m. The council's external auditor, KPMG, reports in its interim annual report that the increase came mainly from high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities, and grew broadly in line with the council's budgeted position.

The council estimates the government's new High Needs Stability Grant could provide about £88.3m, leaving an estimated £8.0m of the historic deficit to be met locally. The grant replaces the Safety Valve programme from 1 April 2026 and covers up to 90% of the cumulative deficit at 31 March 2026, subject to an approved Local SEND Reform Plan. The statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, has been extended to the end of 2027-28. The council's June 2026 SEND Reform data submission forecast an in-year deficit of £63.3m for 2026-27, against £33.4m in 2025-26. The grant was due to be confirmed in October 2026; the papers do not record the outcome. The council's risk register records £7.5m held in reserves.

KPMG retains one weakness from the prior year: a continuing significant weakness in value-for-money arrangements for governance of the schools grant. It says governance and monitoring strengthened during 2025-26 but had not yet shown that high needs pressures were under sustainable control at 31 March 2026.

news_drafts.headline: Cambridgeshire Pension Fund: KPMG sets £49m materiality for its 2025-26 audit
news_drafts.lead:
Cambridgeshire Pension Fund's external auditor, the accountancy firm KPMG, has set materiality for its audit of the fund's 2025-26 accounts at £49m. Materiality is the size of error that an auditor treats as large enough to matter to a reader of the accounts. The Pension Fund Board noted the audit plan at its meeting on 3 July 2026, and the minutes record: "Materiality had been set at £49 million."

KPMG calculated the figure as 1% of the fund's total draft assets as at 31 March 2025. Its plan lists two significant risks: management override of controls, and the valuation of level three assets, which are investments with no quoted market price.

According to the minutes, officers do not expect material differences on the fund's private equity investments.

findings.paper_title: Procurement of Asbestos Analytical and Remediation Services
findings.headline: The paper gives two different expiry dates for the asbestos removal framework: December 2028 in paragraph 2.2 and December 2027 in paragraph 4.2.
findings.detail: Paragraph 2.2 states the removal and demolition framework does not expire until December 2028 and is outside this procurement. Paragraph 4.2, describing Option 2, states the same framework remains available until December 2027 and that the Authority has no minimum spend commitment under it.
findings.matters: A reader working out how long removal spend is covered by existing contracts needs to know which of the two dates applies, and the paper does not reconcile them.
findings.quote: The separate framework for asbestos removal and demolition services does not expire until December 2028

findings.paper_title: Procurement of Asbestos Analytical and Remediation Services
findings.headline: The existing asbestos surveying and consultancy framework expires on 28 February 2027, and the replacement contract's target commencement is 1 June 2027.
findings.detail: The paper says survey work beyond February 2027 will either be commissioned in advance or delivered through the new contracts, with no anticipated interruption. It also says the timetable is challenging and that existing arrangements remain available as a contingency during any transition period.
findings.matters: There is about a three-month gap between the framework expiry and the target start date, and the paper relies on contingency access to existing arrangements to cover it, which another council managing a similar exit would want to check.
findings.figures: 28 February 2027 framework expiry; 1 June 2027 target commencement
findings.quote: The Council's existing framework for asbestos surveying and consultancy services expires on 28 February 2027

findings.paper_title: Procurement of Asbestos Analytical and Remediation Services
findings.headline: Cambridgeshire seeks approval for maximum asbestos contract values of £3 million over a 4-year term, which the paper says exceed historic expenditure levels.
findings.detail: The paper proposes a maximum of £2 million for surveying, consultancy and analytical services and £1 million for removal and remediation, ex-VAT. It attributes the increase to a more proactive approach with more surveying and re-inspection, and says the values are maximum limits rather than committed spend. The paper gives no historic expenditure figure to compare against.
findings.matters: A finance director can see that planned asbestos spend is set above past levels, but the paper gives no baseline figure, so the size of the increase cannot be measured from the document.

findings.headline: Council education officers confirm North Cambridge Academy has space to expand by two forms of entry (300 places), in reply to a query on the Bellerby's site land earmarked for redevelopment.
findings.detail: The letter responds to a request for assurance that the Bellerby's site is not required for expansion of North Cambridge Academy. It states that officers from the Education Capital and Place Planning Team and Meridian Academy Trust have confirmed there will be sufficient space for a further two forms of entry, and that this is the maximum expansion the council considers necessary for demand from known catchment developments.
findings.matters: A disposal or redevelopment of council land is only as clear as the confirmation that the site is not needed for other council service purposes, and a finance director at another council would want to see how that check was documented.
findings.quote: Meridian Academy Trust have provided assurance that there will be sufficient space to expand the school by a further two forms of entry (300 places).

findings.paper_title: Disposal of Land Formerly Known as Bellerby’s College Cambridge
findings.headline: Seven written bids from six parties were received for the site, and the paper recommends award to Bidder 1 with an equal sum offer from Bidder 2 found to have markedly less favourable terms.
findings.detail: The site was marketed by a local agent for seven weeks to 3 July 2026. Shortlisted bidders were interviewed and final offers sought. The paper says Bidder 2's equal sum was assessed as markedly less favourable on terms, producing a significant difference in net present value.
findings.matters: The paper shows how a council documents best consideration under s123 when two bids are equal in headline sum, which is a test other councils may apply to their own disposal decisions.
findings.figures: 7 written bids; 6 parties; shortlist of 4 bidders
findings.quote: 7 written bids from 6 parties were received (one bidder made both a conditional and unconditional offer).
